title: IRDAI's May 25 Circular on Executive Pay: Six Mandatory Parameters Carry 50% of Variable Pay, Including Claims, Grievances and Dark Patterns
summary: IRDAI's circular of May 25, 2026, amending the 2024 Master Circular on Corporate Governance for Insurers, makes six performance parameters, covering financial soundness, product performance, claims responsiveness, grievance redressal, Indian Accounting Standards and removal of dark patterns, account for 50% of key managerial personnel variable pay from FY 2026-27 and requires public disclosure of the underlying data.
description:
India's insurance regulator has told insurers that the way they pay their most senior people must reflect how well they treat policyholders. The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India issued a circular dated May 25, 2026 that amends its Master Circular on Corporate Governance for Insurers, 2024. Outlook Money reported it on May 27, saying the changes apply from the 2026-27 financial year, and Legitpro Law summarised it for Mondaq on June 3. The circular is therefore a late-May measure, ahead of the 2026-27 pay cycle it is meant to shape. The Mondaq article does not reproduce the circular or give a circular reference number, so the details here come from that and other published summaries.

The core of the change is a scorecard for key management personnel, the senior executives such as the chief executive and heads of key functions. According to Mondaq, six mandatory parameters together account for fifty percent of the total assessment used for variable pay and incentives. The six are overall financial soundness, product performance, claims responsiveness, grievance redressal, implementation of Indian Accounting Standards, and the removal of dark patterns in insurer and distributor interactions with customers. Outlook Money gives the weights of two of them, 10% each for implementing Indian Accounting Standards and for removing dark patterns, and says the remaining 50% of the variable pay weighting is set by insurers according to their business priorities and each executive's role. It names the factors for evaluating executives as speed of claim settlement, responsiveness to policyholders, grievance resolution efficiency and product performance. Neither summary gives the weights of the other parameters.

Dark patterns are website or app designs that can confuse customers or steer them into decisions they would not otherwise make. Including them in the executive scorecard puts the digital sales process, which has been a source of complaints, within the leadership's responsibility.

The circular also forces disclosure. Outlook Money reports that insurers must publish data on claims, such as the share of claims settled within 15, 30 and 60 days and beyond, and how many were fully paid, partially paid, rejected, repudiated or still pending. They must publish complaints resolved within set timelines and those still unresolved. Routine service requests and grievances should be kept separate, and a service request unresolved for more than seven days may need to be treated as a grievance. Claims, product performance and grievance data must be published monthly, and financial soundness data quarterly, on the insurer's website in a simple, accessible format, without requiring visitors to provide personal details. Mondaq adds that insurers must disclose the parameters behind executive remuneration, publicly report performance against them and make historical data available in an accessible format.

The metrics differ by type of insurer. For life insurers, Outlook Money lists renewal premium ratios, persistency levels, expense management and assets under management. For general and standalone health insurers, it lists incurred loss ratios, renewal business ratios and expense management indicators. Mondaq notes that sector-specific financial metrics now apply to life, general and health insurers, without giving figures. Persistency, a measure of how many customers keep their policies, appears in the earlier framework and not among the revised mandatory parameters in the Mondaq summary, though Outlook Money lists it for life insurers' disclosure.

Governance is part of the design. Boards and remuneration committees must show that executive incentives reflect policyholder interests, conduct risk and long-term governance objectives. Outlook Money adds that nomination and remuneration committees must coordinate with risk management committees when designing senior management pay. The summaries do not state a penalty for non-compliance, and they do not state deferral or clawback rules for variable pay, so those points should be checked in the circular itself.

The reaction in published coverage is limited. Outlook Money attributes a view to unnamed industry experts that the move could push insurers to improve customer servicing, since weak claim settlement or rising unresolved complaints may now affect executive incentives, and it quotes no named person or insurer. Law-firm commentary frames the circular as a form of indirect enforcement: instead of fining the company, the regulator changes what executives are rewarded for. Critics of such an approach could argue that pay set by regulator-defined measures reduces companies' commercial discretion, but the summaries reviewed do not record a named critic.

The design also reflects a view that conduct problems in insurance are partly incentive problems. When bonuses depend mainly on growth or profit, weaker claims handling or complaint resolution can look like a cost saving, and a scorecard that carries service measures changes that calculation for the people deciding how resources are allocated. Whether it works will depend on how rigorously boards score executives against the published data. For policyholders, the visible effect should be data. Once the monthly claims and grievance figures appear on insurers' websites, comparing insurers becomes easier. For insurers, the immediate work is building the scorecard, the reporting pipeline and the board oversight before the financial year's pay decisions. Readers who need the exact weights, definitions and transition rules should read the circular itself.
source_name: Mondaq (June 3, 2026), Outlook Money (May 27, 2026) and law-firm commentary on the IRDAI circular of May 25, 2026

key_points: IRDAI issued the circular on May 25, 2026, amending its Master Circular on Corporate Governance for Insurers, 2024; Outlook Money reports the changes apply from FY 2026-27.

Six mandatory parameters together make up 50% of the assessment used for variable pay: overall financial soundness, product performance, claims responsiveness, grievance redressal, implementation of Indian Accounting Standards and removal of dark patterns; the other 50% is set by insurers.

Insurers must publish claims data, such as the share settled within 15, 30 and 60 days and beyond, and the number paid, partly paid, rejected, repudiated or pending, monthly, and financial soundness data quarterly, on their websites without asking users for personal details.

Boards and nomination and remuneration committees must show that executive incentives reflect policyholder interests, conduct risk and long-term governance and coordinate with risk management committees.

Sector metrics differ: life insurers report items such as renewal premium ratios, persistency and assets under management, while general and standalone health insurers report incurred loss ratios, renewal business ratios and expense indicators.
why_it_matters: Executives respond to how they are paid. By tying half of variable pay to measures that include claims responsiveness and complaint handling, the regulator is trying to make customer outcomes matter to the people who run insurers. The disclosure rules matter as much as the pay rules, because published monthly claims data lets policyholders, journalists and analysts compare insurers. Industry commentary notes the risk of more regulatory involvement in commercial decisions; the circular does not, as summarised, specify deferral or clawback, so how strongly it bites will depend on how boards apply it.

title: MAS Publishes 'SAFR' White Paper With Industry on Runtime Safeguards for AI Agents in Finance: Identity, Controls, a Disposition Engine and Tamper-Evident Audit Logs
summary: On July 3, 2026 the Monetary Authority of Singapore published an industry white paper, 'Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime' (SAFR), developed with financial institutions and fintechs, describing four runtime components that keep AI agents within the mandates and risk limits set by their firms.
description:
Artificial intelligence systems that can carry out tasks on their own, often called AI agents, are starting to appear in finance. They might initiate a payment, rebalance a portfolio or answer a client and take an action on the client's behalf. Singapore's financial regulator has now published a technical blueprint for keeping them under control. According to an analysis by the law firm Rajah & Tann Asia dated July 6, 2026, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) published an industry white paper on July 3, 2026, titled "Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime", abbreviated to SAFR.

It is worth being clear about what SAFR is. The Rajah & Tann article describes it as an industry white paper, developed by MAS together with leading financial institutions and financial technology companies. The sources reviewed do not say whether it is open for formal consultation or whether it sets binding requirements, so it should be read as guidance and a reference design, not as a rule.

The paper's purpose is to give financial institutions real-time safeguards, so that AI agents stay within the mandates, policies and risk boundaries the institutions set. The central idea is that checks should operate at runtime, at the moment an agent proposes an action, rather than relying only on testing before deployment. The paper's own formulation, quoted by Rajah & Tann, is that "no agentic action reaches execution without having been declared, authorised and assessed."

SAFR describes four runtime components that work through what it calls a governance envelope. The first is agent identity. Each proposed action is checked against a registered agent, so that the institution knows which agent is acting and whether it is permitted to act. The second is a controls repository, which is the institution's configurable rulebook: the limits, policies and conditions that apply to agents. The third is a disposition engine, which resolves each action into one of four outcomes: deny, escalate, auto-execute or observe. Escalation is where a human gets involved, so the engine decides which actions can run automatically, which need a person's decision and which must be blocked. The fourth is an audit log, described as a tamper-evident, append-only record of governance decisions. Because entries can only be added and any alteration is detectable, the log allows later review of what an agent did and why it was allowed.

The framework builds on MAS's Project MindForge AI Risk Management toolkit, which connects it to the regulator's wider work on AI. That includes the guidelines on AI risk management that MAS proposed in November 2025, covering governance, an inventory of AI uses, risk materiality assessment and lifecycle controls for generative AI and AI agents, with a proposed 12-month transition period after issue. SAFR can be read as a technical complement to those principles: the guidelines say what a firm should have in place, and the white paper shows one way to build it for agents that act.

The paper identifies use cases: agent-assisted payments and treasury operations, wealth management and advisory workflows, and client engagement. These are areas where an agent's mistake can have direct financial consequences or affect customers, which is why the authorisation and escalation steps matter. The sources do not mention insurance claims or underwriting specifically, though the same design could apply to any regulated firm that deploys agents.

A few things the sources do not report. The article does not describe a regulatory sandbox, specific technical standards, deadlines for firms or enforcement. It does not give details of which institutions took part. Readers should therefore avoid assuming that adopting SAFR is mandatory or that following it would satisfy any regulatory requirement; that is a question for MAS and the firms' own supervisors.

Why does the approach matter? Traditional AI models produce predictions or recommendations that a person then acts upon. Agentic systems can carry out the next step, which raises questions of accountability, control and auditability. If an agent makes a payment error, a firm needs to know which agent acted, under whose authority and according to which rule. The design separates the agent from the rulebook that governs it, so that limits can be changed centrally and applied consistently, and it records decisions in a way that is hard to alter. A tamper-evident log is especially useful for regulators and auditors, who must reconstruct events after an incident.

Singapore's approach is consistent with its stated preference for principles-based supervision combined with practical industry collaboration. By publishing a reference design with industry participants, MAS offers a common vocabulary that firms can adopt or adapt, and signals the kind of controls it expects to see as agents spread. For firms elsewhere, including insurers and banks in jurisdictions that have not yet issued specific guidance, SAFR provides a concrete example of what runtime governance can look like.

The practical next steps for firms considering agents are to inventory where agents are used or planned, decide which actions an agent may take on its own, define the escalation triggers, and make sure logs are kept in a form that supports audit. Whether MAS follows the white paper with formal guidance or supervisory expectations is something to watch.
source_name: Rajah & Tann Asia (analysis of the MAS white paper, July 6, 2026) and Monetary Authority of Singapore

key_points: MAS published the white paper 'Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime' (SAFR) on July 3, 2026, developed with leading financial institutions and fintech companies; it is a white paper, not a rulebook.
SAFR describes four runtime components working through a 'governance envelope': agent identity, a controls repository, a disposition engine and an audit log.
The disposition engine resolves each proposed action to deny, escalate, auto-execute or observe, and the audit log is a tamper-evident, append-only record of governance decisions.
The paper states that no agentic action reaches execution without having been declared, authorised and assessed, and it builds on MAS's Project MindForge AI Risk Management toolkit.
Use cases include agent-assisted payments and treasury operations, wealth management and advisory workflows, and client engagement.
why_it_matters: AI agents that can take actions, not just give advice, raise new questions about who is accountable if something goes wrong. SAFR gives banks, insurers and fintechs a concrete design for keeping agents inside approved limits with records that can be audited.
